title: Why MSMEs Engage in Community Corporate Social Responsibility: The Primacy of Moral Motivation in South Africa and Ghana
content: This study investigates the motivations underlying corporate social responsibility (CSR) engagement among micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in South Africa and Ghana, with particular attention to community-oriented CSR. Using a deductive research approach, a cross-sectional survey design and cluster sampling, data were collected from 390 MSMEs comprising 220 firms in Bloemfontein and Kimberley, South Africa, and 170 firms in Sekondi and Takoradi, Ghana. Descriptive statistics and Pearson’s chi-square analysis were employed to examine relationships between CSR motivations and CSR dimensions. The findings reveal that morality emerged as the highest-ranked CSR motivation in both countries, while the business case consistently ranked second. More importantly, morality was the only motivation significantly associated with every community-related CSR activity across both national contexts. Significant relationships were observed between moral motivation and community activities such as bursaries, local employment, disaster relief, volunteerism, support for community organisations and crime prevention. The findings suggest that community-oriented CSR among African MSMEs is primarily rooted in ethical responsibility rather than purely economic, institutional or regulatory considerations. The study advances a Moral-Business CSR Model in which morality acts as the primary catalyst for community engagement, while business benefits reinforce and sustain responsible behaviour over time. This contributes to CSR theory and offers important implications for policy and MSME development.
